metadata.research_goal: Synthesize backend-ready swimming event programming and periodization knowledge for sprint, middle-distance, distance, individual medley, open-water, and triathlon swim contexts, including pacing, training zones, set design, volume and intensity progression, tapering, competition week, and beginner/intermediate/advanced adjustment without copying exact copyrighted programs.
metadata.scope: Pool and open-water event programming. Stroke mechanics, starts, turns, injury rehab, and learn-to-swim content are included only where they directly affect event planning, safety gates, training load, pacing, or progression.
metadata.current_rules_note: Rule references were checked on 2026-06-23. Backend race-rule logic should keep competition-governing-body settings configurable because meet, federation, pool-course, open-water, and triathlon rules can differ.
metadata.synthesis_note: Records are original synthesis from federation resources, coaching education, and peer-reviewed sport-science literature. Set examples are represented as patterns and constraints, not copied programs.

source_refs.title: World Aquatics Competition Regulations, Version February 2026
source_refs.evidence_use: Swimming and open-water competition context, event legality, race environment, and need for configurable rule sets.
source_refs.reliability_notes: Primary international governing-body source. Use current version by event date.

source_refs.title: USA Swimming ADM Competence Progressions
source_refs.evidence_use: Developmental progression, threshold awareness, stroke rate and distance-per-stroke education, speed control, and event-readiness concepts.
source_refs.reliability_notes: Official USA Swimming athlete-development material; use as a progression framework rather than a fixed workout prescription.

source_refs.title: Joint Statement on Hypoxic Blackout and Inaccurate Use of the Terminology Shallow Water Blackout
source_refs.organization_or_author: American Red Cross, USA Swimming, YMCA of the USA
source_refs.evidence_use: Safety limits for breath-holding, hyperventilation, underwater swimming, and hypoxic blackout risk.
source_refs.reliability_notes: Authoritative safety guidance for swimming instruction and training environments.

source_refs.title: Advice on Holding Your Breath in Training
source_refs.evidence_use: Practical breath-holding guardrails, supervision requirements, and warning against repeated/prolonged underwater breath-hold work.
source_refs.reliability_notes: Federation safety article; use for backend safety gates in pool and underwater prescriptions.

source_refs.title: Training Zones in Competitive Swimming: A Biophysical Approach
source_refs.evidence_use: Low, moderate, heavy, severe, and extreme swimming intensity domains using VO2 kinetics, lactate, heart rate, RPE, stroke frequency, stroke length, and training-method mapping.
source_refs.reliability_notes: Recent peer-reviewed synthesis; values are most applicable to trained front-crawl swimmers and should be individualized.

source_refs.title: Elite Swimmers' Training Patterns in the 25 Weeks Prior to Their Season's Best Performances
source_refs.organization_or_author: Hellard, Avalos-Fernandes, Lefort, Pla, Mujika, Toussaint, and Pyne
source_refs.evidence_use: Twenty-season elite cohort; intensity distribution, 14-15 week macrocycle patterns, progressive load increases, and sprint/middle-distance periodization signals.
source_refs.reliability_notes: Elite retrospective data; translate conservatively for non-elite users.

source_refs.title: Identifying Optimal Overload and Taper in Elite Swimmers over Time
source_refs.organization_or_author: Hellard, Avalos, Lacoste, Barale, Chatard, and Millet
source_refs.evidence_use: Final six-week overload and taper load-shape modeling; slow-decay taper concepts and individualized evolution across athlete careers.
source_refs.reliability_notes: Elite modeling study; use for taper principles, not rigid percentages for all swimmers.

source_refs.title: Effect of the Pre-Taper Level of Fatigue on the Taper-Induced Changes in Performance in Elite Swimmers
source_refs.evidence_use: Pre-taper fatigue, sleep quality, taper response, and the practical need to individualize taper reductions.
source_refs.reliability_notes: Elite/national sample; useful for backend readiness and sleep/fatigue modifiers.

source_refs.title: Training Regimes and Recovery Monitoring Practices of Elite British Swimmers
source_refs.organization_or_author: Stangier, Abel, Hesse, Claen, Mierau, Hollmann, Struder, and Donath
source_refs.evidence_use: Event-specific weekly load differences across sprint, middle, and long-distance swimmers; session terminology and recovery-monitoring practice.
source_refs.reliability_notes: Small elite sample; use as a specificity signal rather than universal volume target.

source_refs.title: The Variability of Competitive Performance and Pacing Strategies in Different Rounds of the 400 m and 800 m Freestyle Swimming Races at the 2017-2024 World Swimming Championships
source_refs.evidence_use: Middle-distance freestyle heat/final pacing, finalist performance changes, medalist positioning, and 400/800 pacing profiles.
source_refs.reliability_notes: Elite championship analysis; useful for advanced competition-week pacing decisions.

source_refs.title: Pacing Strategy of 800 m and 1500 m Freestyle Swimming Finals in the World Championships According to the Performance in Males and Females of Different Age Groups
source_refs.evidence_use: 800 m and 1500 m U-shaped pacing, split variability, age/sex/performance-level differences, and distance-specific pacing skill development.
source_refs.reliability_notes: Observational finals data; use to create individual pacing templates, not universal split mandates.

source_refs.title: Race Strategies of Open Water Swimmers in the 5-km, 10-km, and 25-km Races of the 2017 FINA World Swimming Championships
source_refs.evidence_use: Open-water pacing and tactical positioning by race distance and sex; negative pacing and late-race speed increase among successful swimmers.
source_refs.reliability_notes: Elite championship context; account for course, field size, water conditions, and pack behavior.

source_refs.title: How to Draft in Open Water Races
source_refs.evidence_use: Practical open-water drafting skills, bilateral breathing, catch-the-draft sprint tolerance, and race preparation.
source_refs.reliability_notes: Coaching guidance for adult swimmers; pair with peer-reviewed pacing literature.

source_refs.title: World Triathlon Competition Rules Documents
source_refs.evidence_use: Triathlon swim-segment context, competition rules, wetsuit/water-condition configurability, and transition-aware planning.
source_refs.reliability_notes: Primary international triathlon rule repository; event directors may publish race-specific modifications.

source_refs.title: Does Pool Performance of Elite Triathletes Predict Open-Water Performance?
source_refs.evidence_use: Relationship between graded pool lactate-test variables and triathlon open-water swim segment performance.
source_refs.reliability_notes: Elite triathlon sample; useful for triathlon swim benchmarks while still requiring open-water skill work.

source_refs.title: Shoulder Pain and Injury Risk Factors in Competitive Swimmers: A Systematic Review
source_refs.evidence_use: Shoulder risk factors including workload spikes, posterior shoulder strength endurance, and technique quality.
source_refs.reliability_notes: Best used for load-risk flags and prevention logic, not diagnosis.

source_refs.title: Swim-Training Volume and Shoulder Pain Across the Life Span of the Competitive Swimmer
source_refs.evidence_use: Training-volume relationship to shoulder pain, especially in adolescent competitive swimmers.
source_refs.reliability_notes: Supports conservative weekly-volume progression and symptom tracking.

source_refs.title: Epidemiology of Injuries and Prevention Strategies in Competitive Swimmers
source_refs.evidence_use: Common swimming injury sites, overuse mechanisms, and prevention themes for shoulder, back, knee, and training-load management.
source_refs.reliability_notes: Clinical review; use for risk categories and referral flags, not medical advice.

key_concepts.name: Event Specificity Beats Generic Yardage
key_concepts.summary: Swimming programs must change by event duration, stroke, pool versus open-water context, competition schedule, and athlete level. The same weekly yardage can mean different things depending on intensity, stroke distribution, rest, equipment, and technical quality.
key_concepts.backend_translation: Require event_family, stroke_focus, pool_or_open_water, current_continuous_distance, weekly_frequency, injury_history, and goal_date before selecting programming records.

key_concepts.name: Speed Is Drag-Limited
key_concepts.summary: Because water resistance rises steeply with speed, small pacing errors and technical breakdowns can cause large energy costs. Event plans must protect body position, stroke length, breathing rhythm, and turns or sighting under fatigue.
key_concepts.backend_translation: Tie intensity progression to technique stability markers rather than pace alone.

key_concepts.name: Training Zones Need Physiological and Technical Inputs
key_concepts.summary: Useful swim zones combine pace, RPE, lactate or threshold proxies, heart-rate response, stroke rate, stroke length, and ability to hold mechanics. Pace-only zones are incomplete when technique collapses.
key_concepts.backend_translation: Store zone prescriptions with target_effort, target_pace_relation, rest_style, technique_constraint, and stop_condition.

key_concepts.name: Low-Intensity Volume Is Useful When Technical
key_concepts.summary: Elite data show most total swimming in successful programs occurs at or below threshold-like intensities, but easy work must still carry technical intent, rhythm, and efficient repeats.
key_concepts.backend_translation: Generate aerobic volume as technique-constrained swimming, not unfocused filler.

key_concepts.name: High Intensity Has Small Volume and High Cost
key_concepts.summary: Severe, extreme, sprint, and lactate-tolerance work creates large neuromuscular, metabolic, and technical stress from relatively low yardage. It should be protected with rest, recovery, and level gates.
key_concepts.backend_translation: Cap weekly high_intensity_repeat_volume separately from total swim volume.

key_concepts.name: Sprint Training Is Quality, Power, and Skill
key_concepts.summary: 50 and 100 m swimmers need start/turn speed, maximal velocity, alactic power, race-specific breathing choices, and technical stiffness. High fatigue that destroys speed is rarely sprint-specific.
key_concepts.backend_translation: Prefer short repeats, high rest, fast mechanics, and full-recovery speed blocks for sprint goals.

key_concepts.name: Middle Distance Is a Bridge Between Speed and Endurance
key_concepts.summary: 200 and 400 m events require enough aerobic support to resist fade, enough anaerobic capacity to tolerate race pace, and enough speed to stay competitive through early and late segments.
key_concepts.backend_translation: Blend aerobic base, threshold, race-pace fragments, lactate tolerance, and speed maintenance inside the block.

key_concepts.name: Distance Swimming Requires Economy, Pacing, and Finish Speed
key_concepts.summary: 800 and 1500 m pool races depend on sustainable rhythm, low split variability, threshold capacity, stroke economy, and a controlled final-speed reserve.
key_concepts.backend_translation: Distance records should train pace locks, split feedback, threshold durability, negative or U-shaped pacing, and late-race surges.

key_concepts.name: IM Is Four-Stroke Programming, Not Freestyle With Extras
key_concepts.summary: Individual medley planning needs stroke balance, transition skill, stroke-specific load control, and fatigue management because butterfly, backstroke, breaststroke, and freestyle stress different tissues and energy demands.
key_concepts.backend_translation: Track stroke-specific volume and risk flags for fly/back loading, breaststroke knee/groin load, and IM transition practice.

key_concepts.name: Open Water Is Endurance Plus Navigation and Pack Tactics
key_concepts.summary: Open-water swimmers need aerobic durability, variable pace, sighting, drafting, contact tolerance, buoy turns, environmental judgment, and late-race positioning.
key_concepts.backend_translation: Open-water blocks require skill exposures beyond pool pace sets, including sighting frequency, drafting comfort, and environmental safety checks.

key_concepts.name: Triathlon Swim Must Protect the Bike and Run
key_concepts.summary: Triathlon swim performance depends on pool fitness and open-water skill, but the best swim plan also considers drafting, wetsuit rules, start density, transition, and energy cost for later disciplines.
key_concepts.backend_translation: Triathlon swim workouts should include open-water skills, controlled starts, race-intensity economy, and downstream fatigue notes.

key_concepts.name: Pacing Is Trainable
key_concepts.summary: Race pacing improves when athletes connect target splits, perceived effort, breathing rhythm, stroke rate, stroke length, and fatigue signals. Regular split feedback is a programming requirement, not a race-week detail.
key_concepts.backend_translation: Include pacing_skill objective in middle-distance, distance, open-water, triathlon, and advanced sprint blocks.

key_concepts.name: Taper Is Fatigue Reduction With Sharpness Retained
key_concepts.summary: Effective tapering reduces training load enough to recover while preserving intensity, water feel, starts/turns, and race rhythm. Overreached swimmers may need a larger or earlier reduction than acutely fatigued swimmers.
key_concepts.backend_translation: Taper records should modify volume, high-intensity density, dryland load, sleep priority, and race-specific rehearsal by event and fatigue status.

key_concepts.name: Level Gates Prevent Unsafe Programming
key_concepts.summary: Beginners need water confidence, breathing, floating, and short rest-rich practice before fitness volume. Intermediate swimmers can add structure and pacing. Advanced swimmers can tolerate race-pace and lactate work if technique and recovery are stable.
key_concepts.backend_translation: Do not assign high volume, hypoxic work, diving, heavy fly volume, or lactate sets to swimmers who fail readiness gates.

model.sprint_50_100: maximal velocity, start/turn/underwater quality, alactic power, race-specific breathing, full-recovery speed
model.middle_200_400: race-pace control, aerobic support, anaerobic tolerance, speed reserve, segment rehearsal
model.distance_800_1500: threshold durability, economical stroke, split control, negative or U-shaped pacing, late-race surge
model.individual_medley: four-stroke technical capacity, transition turns, stroke-order pacing, stroke-specific load control
model.open_water: sustained aerobic rhythm, sighting, drafting, buoy turns, variable pace, environmental safety
model.triathlon_swim: open-water economy, pack navigation, drafting, wetsuit context, transition and bike/run preservation

model.low: easy aerobic capacity below threshold; long duration or extensive intervals; technique should stay relaxed
model.moderate: around aerobic/anaerobic threshold; durable aerobic pressure; still controlled and repeatable
model.heavy: above threshold with progressive lactate and oxygen slow-component stress; useful for threshold and distance race fragments
model.severe: near VO2max/aerobic power; very hard, limited duration, requires careful recovery
model.extreme: above VO2max intensity; sprint and anaerobic capacity work with complete or near-complete recovery

technical_models.name: Stroke Quality Constraint Model
technical_models.model: A set is only appropriate if the swimmer can hold the intended stroke mechanics, breathing rhythm, body line, and pace objective. When stroke count rises sharply, breathing becomes panicked, shoulders become symptomatic, or pace fades beyond the set purpose, the backend should shorten, rest, or downgrade intensity.

model.repeat_distance: shorter for speed/technique, longer for threshold and endurance, mixed for race segmentation
model.repeat_count: scaled by level, stroke, current volume, event, and fatigue state
model.sendoff_or_rest: sets density; full recovery for speed, short/controlled rest for aerobic and threshold
model.target: pace, RPE, stroke count, stroke rate, distance per stroke, breathing pattern, tactical skill, or split consistency
model.equipment: fins, paddles, pull buoy, snorkel, tempo device, or wetsuit only when it supports the objective and does not hide a problem
model.stop_rule: terminate or modify if safety, pain, breath control, or technique gates fail

technical_models.name: Weekly Microcycle Polarity
technical_models.model: Most swimmers need a weekly rhythm that separates high-intensity race-pace, speed, threshold, aerobic technical volume, recovery, and dryland. Sprint swimmers protect quality speed; middle and distance swimmers carry more threshold/aerobic work; open-water and triathlon swimmers include skill and continuous rhythm.

technical_models.name: Volume Progression Guardrail
technical_models.model: Progress volume gradually by increasing one major stressor at a time: frequency, total distance, intensity density, stroke-specific volume, or resistance-tool use. Add deload or consolidation weeks when symptoms, sleep, or pace quality degrade.

technical_models.name: Intensity Density Progression
technical_models.model: Advance intensity by first improving execution at current pace, then adding repetitions, then reducing rest or increasing target pace. Do not increase pace and density at the same time for swimmers with unstable technique or symptom flags.

technical_models.name: Sprint Periodization Model
technical_models.model: Sprint blocks progress from technical speed and alactic quality, to race-phase segmentation, to race-pace integration and taper. Aerobic work supports recovery and skill, but the key session currency is fast, accurate swimming with enough rest.

technical_models.name: Middle-Distance Periodization Model
technical_models.model: Middle-distance blocks progress from aerobic and technical base, to threshold and race-pace fragments, to event-specific segment rehearsal and taper. The athlete must learn how each race segment should feel.

technical_models.name: Distance Periodization Model
technical_models.model: Distance blocks prioritize aerobic volume, threshold durability, split consistency, efficiency under fatigue, and controlled late-race speed. Race pace should be approached through repeatable fragments before long sustained efforts.

technical_models.name: Individual Medley Periodization Model
technical_models.model: IM blocks need stroke distribution, transition turns, order-specific pacing, and tissue load balancing. Butterfly volume and breaststroke kick load require explicit caps, while freestyle closing work should be trained under accumulated stroke fatigue.

technical_models.name: Open-Water Periodization Model
technical_models.model: Open-water blocks progress from pool endurance and sighting basics, to variable-pace and drafting skill, to race-specific starts, buoy turns, pack positioning, environmental practice, and late-race speed.

technical_models.name: Triathlon Swim Periodization Model
technical_models.model: Triathlon swim blocks combine pool pace benchmarks, open-water navigation, pack/draft decisions, wetsuit adaptation when legal, and transition-aware energy management. Training should include swim-to-bike context for intermediate and advanced triathletes.

model.50_100: fast start and maximal speed with technical breathing plan; avoid turning breath restriction into unsafe hypoxic challenges
model.200: controlled first half, protected third quarter, aggressive finish if stroke mechanics remain intact
model.400_800: advanced swimmers may use event-specific U-shaped, fast-start-even, or negative profiles based on heats/finals and strength profile
model.1500: low split variability with a planned last segment lift
model.open_water: field-dependent pacing with pack placement, draft opportunities, buoy congestion, and final acceleration
model.triathlon: controlled opening, efficient middle, tactical draft/sighting, and exit readiness for transition

technical_models.name: Taper Decision Model
technical_models.model: Choose taper length and reduction by event, training age, fatigue level, meet priority, and recent load. Maintain race-specific intensity and feel while reducing total load and dryland fatigue. Overreached swimmers need earlier and larger recovery emphasis than swimmers with normal acute fatigue.

technical_models.name: Competition Week Model
technical_models.model: Competition week prioritizes sleep, hydration, familiar warm-ups, event-specific pace touches, starts/turns or open-water skill cues, low extra volume, and no new equipment or technique overhaul. Multi-event meets need heat/final and event-spacing load management.

model.beginner: water confidence, breathing, floating, short repeats, long rest, technique gates, no hypoxic challenges, no high-volume race sets
model.intermediate: structured aerobic work, basic zones, pacing education, drill-to-swim integration, moderate volume progression, simple race-pace fragments
model.advanced: event-specific zones, speed and lactate tolerance, individual pacing templates, taper, multi-session weekly planning, and detailed load tracking

technical_models.name: Swim Load Monitoring Model
technical_models.model: Track total weekly swim distance, session RPE, high-intensity repeat distance, stroke-specific distance, paddles/fins/pull-buoy exposure, dryland load, shoulder/back/knee symptoms, sleep, and pace quality. Decisions should use trends, not a single metric.

tactical_rules.rule: For 50 m sprint events, prioritize start, breakout, maximal speed, clean turn if applicable, and technical line. The race plan should be simple enough to execute under maximal arousal.
tactical_rules.do_not_do: Do not prescribe repeated no-breath challenges or extended underwater breath-hold work as a substitute for safe race-specific breathing and underwater skill.

tactical_rules.rule: For 100 m events, balance aggressive opening speed with the ability to maintain stroke length and kick/turn quality on the second half.
tactical_rules.backend_cue: Use split review to flag swimmers who open too fast and lose stroke length or who open too conservatively and cannot access top speed.

tactical_rules.rule: For 200 m events, train the swimmer to avoid an uncontrolled first 50, protect the third 50, and finish with mechanics intact.
tactical_rules.backend_cue: Use race-pace fragments with enough rest to rehearse segment feel before using fatigue-tolerance sets.

tactical_rules.rule: For 400 and 800 m freestyle, choose the pacing template from the athlete's profile and round context. Advanced finalists may need a U-shaped or fast-start-even model, while developing swimmers often need smoother split control first.
tactical_rules.backend_cue: Require recent split data before prescribing advanced tactical profiles.

tactical_rules.rule: For 1500 m freestyle, prioritize sustainable rhythm, low split variability, and a planned final-speed lift rather than repeated abrupt surges.
tactical_rules.backend_cue: Train pace lock and perceived effort calibration before tactical surges.

tactical_rules.rule: In meets with heats and finals, never assume the heat is a full taper-effort race or a throwaway. The goal is to qualify safely while preserving the ability to improve in the final.
tactical_rules.backend_cue: For advanced swimmers, competition-week records should include heat/final split strategy and recovery between swims.

tactical_rules.rule: In IM, butterfly should be fast enough to stay in the race but controlled enough to avoid destroying backstroke and breaststroke mechanics.
tactical_rules.backend_cue: Flag fly-dominant opening patterns that cause back half collapse.

tactical_rules.rule: Breaststroke leg in IM deserves specific pacing and load management because it can be decisive while also increasing knee/groin stress.
tactical_rules.backend_cue: Track breaststroke kick exposure separately from total swim volume.

tactical_rules.rule: IM freestyle closing work should be practiced after prior-stroke fatigue, not only as fresh freestyle.
tactical_rules.backend_cue: Use medley-fragment patterns rather than only straight freestyle race-pace sets.

tactical_rules.rule: Open-water starts require a controlled acceleration that secures useful position without creating unsustainable lactate or panic.
tactical_rules.backend_cue: Train short start surges followed by settling into race rhythm.

tactical_rules.rule: Drafting should be trained as a skill: catch the draft, relax in it, breathe to both sides, and verify navigation rather than blindly trusting another swimmer.
tactical_rules.backend_cue: Include drafting skill only when group/open-water supervision is available; use pool simulations otherwise.

tactical_rules.rule: Buoy turns are tactical choke points. Swimmers should practice choosing a tight, moderate, or wider line based on traffic, ability, and goal.
tactical_rules.backend_cue: Do not introduce contact-heavy buoy tactics to anxious beginners before basic open-water comfort.

tactical_rules.rule: Successful open-water swimmers often preserve or increase pace late. Training should include controlled finishing speed after sustained rhythm.
tactical_rules.backend_cue: Use late-race surge objectives sparingly and only after aerobic durability exists.

tactical_rules.rule: Triathlon swim pacing should seek the fastest sustainable swim that preserves transition, bike, and run execution, not necessarily the fastest isolated swim split.
tactical_rules.backend_cue: Attach downstream fatigue notes to triathlon swim workouts.

tactical_rules.rule: Triathletes should sight often enough to stay on course but not so often that body position and rhythm collapse.
tactical_rules.backend_cue: Progress sighting from low-stress pool or calm-water practice to race-pace integration.

tactical_rules.rule: If a wetsuit is likely legal and used, practice in it before race week to adapt shoulder feel, body position, kick pattern, buoyancy, and exit routine.
tactical_rules.backend_cue: Keep wetsuit legality configurable by event rules and water temperature.

tactical_rules.rule: Pacing sets should give feedback on split, stroke count, perceived effort, and breathing rhythm so the swimmer learns the sensation of target pace.
tactical_rules.backend_cue: For intermediate and advanced users, include planned feedback intervals inside pace sets.

tactical_rules.rule: Race week is for confidence, rhythm, speed touches, and recovery. Do not overhaul stroke technique, equipment, breathing pattern, or starts late unless required for safety.
tactical_rules.backend_cue: Block new high-complexity drills and new equipment tags in competition week.

tactical_rules.rule: Hard sets stop being useful when the athlete misses the target purpose: repeated major pace misses, visible stroke collapse, sharp pain, panic breathing, dizziness, or unsafe underwater behavior.
tactical_rules.backend_cue: Every high-intensity record should include a downgrade path and stop condition.

tactical_rules.rule: Beginners should not receive event-specific race-pace training until they can breathe rhythmically, recover to stand or safe float, complete repeat lengths calmly, and understand lane safety.
tactical_rules.backend_cue: Route beginner event goals through water-confidence and basic continuous-swim records first.

physical_demands.why_it_matters: Supports technical volume, recovery between repeats, distance events, open-water endurance, and triathlon swim economy.
Allows swimmers to sustain strong pace without early lactate accumulation and supports 400 m through open-water race efforts.
Supports severe-intensity swimming near VO2max, important for 200/400 race segments and hard surges.
Helps 100/200/400 swimmers tolerate hard closing segments but creates high fatigue and technique risk.
Drives maximal velocity, start breakout speed, and sprint skill without needing large repeat volume.
Reduces energy cost per metre and protects pacing, especially as fatigue rises.
Allows swimmers to change speed deliberately rather than by thrashing or shortening the stroke excessively.
Swimming creates repetitive overhead load; shoulder capacity and posterior endurance help tolerate volume and race-pace work.
Supports body line, rotation timing, efficient breathing, butterfly rhythm, underwaters, and open-water sighting stability.
Supports sprint propulsion, body position, dolphin kick, and back-half race stability; excessive kicking can increase knee/back load depending on stroke.
Pool events include repeated acceleration phases. Event programming should not treat swimming as only surface yardage.
Open-water and triathlon swimmers must maintain course direction while preserving stroke rhythm and position.
Open-water starts, buoy turns, and drafting require comfort near other swimmers without panic or reckless effort.
Open-water and triathlon performance can be altered by water temperature, wetsuits, chop, current, sunlight, visibility, and race-day safety rules.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Rapid increases in swim volume can overload the shoulder and degrade technique.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Increase one load variable at a time and use consolidation weeks when symptoms or quality worsen.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Shoulder pain is a central swimming overuse risk, especially with high volume, poor mechanics, poor posterior endurance, and abrupt load changes.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Reduce painful stroke volume, remove paddles early, add recovery, and refer for medical assessment when pain persists.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Paddles and resistance tools can increase shoulder load and hide poor catch mechanics if used too early or too often.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Use small doses only for capable swimmers and remove them during return-to-swim or shoulder irritation.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Breaststroke kick and high breaststroke volume can irritate knees, groin, or hips, especially during IM or breaststroke-specialist blocks.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Progress kick volume gradually and substitute lower-risk stroke/aerobic work during symptoms.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Butterfly volume, dolphin kicking, and fatigued body-wave mechanics can overload shoulders and low back.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Gate butterfly volume by level and stop when rhythm collapses.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Hyperventilation, extended underwater swimming, repeated breath-holding, and max-distance no-breath challenges can cause hypoxic blackout and drowning risk.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Do not prescribe prolonged or repeated breath-hold challenges; require supervision and safe breathing education.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Heavy upper-body dryland close to key swim sessions can reduce stroke quality and increase shoulder fatigue.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Separate heavy upper-body lifting from key race-pace or speed sessions when possible.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Excessive pre-taper fatigue and poor sleep can blunt taper response and impair performance.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Begin recovery earlier and reduce load more decisively when fatigue is high.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Too much hard-but-not-specific swimming can accumulate fatigue without developing clear speed, threshold, or race-pace objectives.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Clarify the purpose of hard sessions and keep easy work easy enough to restore technical quality.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Open-water swimming adds cold/heat exposure, visibility, current, waves, water quality, boat traffic, and rescue-access risks.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Require supervised open-water practice and event-specific safety checks before prescribing open-water sessions.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Beginners and pool-only swimmers may panic in open water or in pack contact, causing breathing disruption and unsafe pacing.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Progress from pool skills to calm supervised open water before race-simulation work.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Wetsuits can alter shoulder feel, body position, temperature, and anxiety; poor fit may increase shoulder or neck discomfort.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Practice in race-legal equipment before race week and adjust stroke/kick rhythm.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Race-pace, threshold, lactate, or open-water pack sets are unsafe or unproductive for swimmers who cannot breathe, float, recover, or complete repeat lengths calmly.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Route to beginner foundation and water-confidence progressions first.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Multi-event meets can create repeated high-intensity exposures, warm-up/cool-down volume, travel fatigue, and sleep disruption.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Plan event priorities, between-race recovery, and post-meet deload.

training_implications.summary: Before generating swim programming, collect level, water confidence, continuous distance, target event, pool length/access, weekly frequency, session duration, stroke familiarity, open-water context, and shoulder/back/knee history.
Beginner swim plans should prioritize comfort, face immersion, exhalation, floating/recovery, short repeats, long rest, and simple freestyle fragments before aerobic workload.
Intermediate swimmers benefit from structured aerobic intervals, technique constraints, simple pace targets, stroke count awareness, and conservative progressions.
Advanced swimmers should be assigned blocks by event family with clear weekly distribution among aerobic, threshold, speed, race pace, recovery, and dryland support.
Every set should have one primary purpose: technical quality, aerobic capacity, threshold, race pace, lactate tolerance, max speed, open-water skill, recovery, or test/assessment.

Pace targets should come from recent ability, threshold/CSS-style testing, race data, or coach-entered benchmarks. Generic pace tables can misclassify swimmers because technique and water skill vary widely.
Race-pace sets require enough rest to hit pace and mechanics. If rest is too short, the set may become lactate tolerance or poor-technique conditioning instead.
Aerobic volume should include relaxed breathing, stable body line, stroke count or stroke-length awareness, and pace consistency rather than only distance accumulation.
Sprint blocks should include short high-quality speed exposures, start/turn skills where safe, and adequate recovery. Large tired sprint sets often train fatigue rather than maximal speed.
200 and 400 m athletes need event segments rehearsed as first-half control, middle-pressure tolerance, and closing speed rather than only continuous conditioning.
800/1500 m swimmers need repeated split feedback, threshold durability, and late-race speed after controlled pace. Abrupt speed changes should be trained deliberately, not accidentally.
IM plans should account for four-stroke competence, transition turns, stroke-order fatigue, and tissue-specific stress, not just total metres.
Open-water preparation should include sighting, drafting, starting, buoy turns, contact tolerance, variable pace, and safety procedures in addition to endurance.
Triathlon swim training should include race-intensity economy, open-water skills, wetsuit/rules context, transition rehearsal, and energy management for the bike and run.
Progressive overload should include deload or consolidation weeks, especially after new frequency, hard-set density, stroke-specific volume, or tool use.
Taper generally reduces total load while preserving event-specific speed, feel, and technical confidence. The exact reduction depends on fatigue, event, age, and training history.
Competition-week sessions should be short enough to recover from, familiar enough to reduce anxiety, and specific enough to maintain race rhythm.
Breathing skills should teach rhythm, exhalation, calmness, and race-appropriate timing. Do not prescribe max-distance no-breath or repeated prolonged underwater breath-holding.
Fins, paddles, pull buoys, snorkels, tempo trainers, and wetsuits should be selected for a clear purpose and constrained by safety, symptoms, and technical transfer.
Dryland should improve shoulder/scapular control, trunk control, posterior chain, mobility, and power without compromising key swim sessions.
Masters and returning swimmers often need more recovery, lower initial volume, cautious high-intensity exposure, and close symptom monitoring even if they have past swim experience.

Use tests that answer programming questions: continuous distance for beginners, threshold/CSS-like pace for endurance, repeatability for race pace, split control for pacing, and symptom response for return-to-swim.
After priority meets or hard open-water races, programming should account for racing, travel, warm-up/cool-down volume, sleep loss, and emotional load before restarting progression.

backend_records_to_create.title: Sprint 50/100 Programming Model
backend_records_to_create.summary: Build around max-speed skill, start/turn quality where safe, alactic repeats, race-specific breathing choices, and enough aerobic support for recovery.

backend_records_to_create.title: 200 m Programming Model
backend_records_to_create.summary: Train speed reserve, controlled opening, race-pace repeatability, lactate tolerance, and a protected third quarter.

backend_records_to_create.title: 400 m Programming Model
backend_records_to_create.summary: Blend threshold, aerobic power, race-pace fragments, and pacing skill so the swimmer can handle fast-but-controlled speed without excessive fade.

backend_records_to_create.title: 800/1500 m Distance Programming Model
backend_records_to_create.summary: Prioritize aerobic capacity, threshold durability, stroke economy, split locking, and late-race speed without abrupt unsustainable surges.

backend_records_to_create.title: Individual Medley Programming Model
backend_records_to_create.summary: Train all four strokes, stroke-order fatigue, transition turns, and load balance rather than adding occasional IM at the end of freestyle work.

backend_records_to_create.title: Open-Water Programming Model
backend_records_to_create.summary: Combine endurance, sighting, drafting, starts, buoy turns, contact tolerance, variable pace, and late-race positioning.

backend_records_to_create.title: Triathlon Swim Programming Model
backend_records_to_create.summary: Develop pool fitness, open-water skills, drafting, sighting, wetsuit adaptation where legal, and energy management for transition, bike, and run.

backend_records_to_create.title: Low Aerobic Capacity Zone
backend_records_to_create.summary: Easy controlled swimming below threshold used for technical volume, recovery, warm-up, beginner endurance, and open-water base.

backend_records_to_create.title: Moderate Aerobic/Threshold Support Zone
backend_records_to_create.summary: Controlled work around threshold support where breathing and technique remain sustainable.

backend_records_to_create.title: Heavy Threshold and Race-Fragment Zone
backend_records_to_create.summary: Above-threshold work that creates progressive fatigue and requires careful dose control.

backend_records_to_create.title: Severe Aerobic Power Zone
backend_records_to_create.summary: Very hard work near aerobic power limits, useful for advanced race segments and surges but costly to recover from.

backend_records_to_create.title: Extreme Anaerobic and Max-Speed Zone
backend_records_to_create.summary: Maximal or near-maximal sprint work requiring high rest, low volume, strict technical quality, and safety guardrails.

backend_records_to_create.title: Technical Aerobic Set Pattern
backend_records_to_create.summary: Use short to moderate repeats or continuous swimming at easy effort with clear technique constraints.

backend_records_to_create.title: Threshold Cruise Set Pattern
backend_records_to_create.summary: Repeated moderate-to-hard aerobic intervals where the swimmer holds a sustainable pace and stable mechanics.

backend_records_to_create.title: Race-Pace Fragment Set Pattern
backend_records_to_create.summary: Break event pace into repeatable fragments with enough rest to preserve target speed and mechanics.

backend_records_to_create.title: Lactate Tolerance Set Pattern
backend_records_to_create.summary: Small doses of hard repeats that teach the swimmer to hold skill under heavy metabolic stress.

backend_records_to_create.title: Max-Speed Set Pattern
backend_records_to_create.summary: Very short, very fast repeats with full recovery and strict stop rules for speed drop or form loss.

backend_records_to_create.title: Recovery Technique Set Pattern
backend_records_to_create.summary: Low-stress swimming used to restore feel, rehearse cues, and maintain water rhythm without adding meaningful fatigue.

backend_records_to_create.title: 200 m Third-Quarter Guardrail
backend_records_to_create.summary: Train the third quarter as a decision point: keep speed close enough to race plan without losing stroke length or breathing control.

backend_records_to_create.title: 400/800 U-Shaped Pacing Option
backend_records_to_create.summary: Advanced 400/800 swimmers may use a controlled fast opening, stable middle, and late lift when split history supports it.

backend_records_to_create.title: 1500 m Smooth-Pace Rule
backend_records_to_create.summary: For 1500 m, train smooth pace control and final lift before tactical surges. The backend should flag erratic split patterns as pacing-skill deficits.

backend_records_to_create.title: Open-Water Negative Finish Rule
backend_records_to_create.summary: Open-water swimmers should learn to settle, hold useful position, and preserve the ability to accelerate late.

backend_records_to_create.title: Triathlon Swim Energy Budget Rule
backend_records_to_create.summary: Choose a swim effort that exits with composure and useful position while preserving bike/run capacity.

backend_records_to_create.title: Beginner Foundation Adjustment
backend_records_to_create.summary: Replace event-specific volume with water confidence, breathing, floating/recovery, short repeats, and easy technique practice.

backend_records_to_create.title: Beginner Continuous-Swim Builder
backend_records_to_create.summary: Build from short repeat lengths to longer continuous swimming only when breathing, body line, and recovery stay calm.

backend_records_to_create.title: Intermediate Structured Aerobic Adjustment
backend_records_to_create.summary: Use structured aerobic intervals with pace, stroke count, breathing rhythm, and simple zone targets instead of random continuous swimming.

backend_records_to_create.title: Intermediate Event-Specific Introduction
backend_records_to_create.summary: Introduce race-specific fragments, split feedback, and light pacing models without advanced lactate density or high-risk stroke volume.

backend_records_to_create.title: Advanced Periodized Block Adjustment
backend_records_to_create.summary: Use multi-week event-specific blocks with planned volume, intensity distribution, dryland placement, testing, taper, and competition-week reduction.

backend_records_to_create.title: Base Phase
backend_records_to_create.summary: Build frequency tolerance, aerobic volume, technical consistency, and strength support before dense race-pace work.

backend_records_to_create.title: Build Phase
backend_records_to_create.summary: Progress intensity density and event-specific work while preserving recovery and technique.

backend_records_to_create.title: Race-Specific Phase
backend_records_to_create.summary: Move from general fitness to event segments, pacing plan, starts/turns or open-water skills, and confidence under race-like fatigue.

backend_records_to_create.title: Swimming Taper Rule
backend_records_to_create.summary: Reduce total load while retaining race-speed touches, technical feel, and confidence. Scale the reduction to event, fatigue, and training history.

backend_records_to_create.title: Competition Week Rule
backend_records_to_create.summary: Use short familiar sessions, event-specific pace touches, technical cues, sleep/recovery emphasis, and clear warm-up/cool-down planning.

backend_records_to_create.title: Post-Competition Absorption Rule
backend_records_to_create.summary: After competition, reduce load enough to absorb racing, travel, warm-up/cool-down volume, sleep disruption, and tissue stress before restarting progression.

backend_records_to_create.title: Open-Water Sighting Progression
backend_records_to_create.summary: Progress sighting from pool rhythm drills to calm-water practice to race-pace sighting under fatigue.

backend_records_to_create.title: Open-Water Drafting Progression
backend_records_to_create.summary: Teach drafting as positioning, effort control, bilateral breathing, and navigation verification rather than passive following.

backend_records_to_create.title: Open-Water Buoy Turn Progression
backend_records_to_create.summary: Practice controlled buoy turns with line choice, contact awareness, acceleration out, and breathing reset.

backend_records_to_create.title: Triathlon Wetsuit Adaptation
backend_records_to_create.summary: When wetsuits are legal and likely, practice fit, shoulder feel, buoyancy, kick change, sighting, and fast removal before race week.

backend_records_to_create.title: Total and Specific Swim Load Monitor
backend_records_to_create.summary: Track total swim distance plus high-intensity, stroke-specific, equipment, dryland, and symptom load because total metres alone misses important stress.

backend_records_to_create.title: Shoulder Load Guardrail
backend_records_to_create.summary: Reduce or modify swimming when shoulder symptoms rise, stroke quality worsens, or resistance-tool volume increases too quickly.

backend_records_to_create.title: Breaststroke Knee and Groin Guardrail
backend_records_to_create.summary: Track breaststroke kick distance and symptoms separately; reduce kick load when knee, groin, or hip irritation appears.

backend_records_to_create.title: Butterfly and Low-Back Guardrail
backend_records_to_create.summary: Cap butterfly and underwater dolphin volume for developing swimmers and reduce exposure when low-back or shoulder symptoms appear.

backend_records_to_create.title: Hypoxic and Breath-Hold Safety Guardrail
backend_records_to_create.summary: Do not prescribe hyperventilation, repeated prolonged breath-holds, max-distance no-breath swimming, or unsupervised underwater challenges.

backend_records_to_create.title: Open-Water Readiness Gate
backend_records_to_create.summary: Require pool competence, calm breathing, continuous swim ability, supervised venue, environmental check, and emergency plan before open-water prescriptions.

backend_records_to_create.title: Continuous Distance and Confidence Assessment
backend_records_to_create.summary: Use the swimmer's calm continuous distance and breathing comfort to choose beginner versus structured aerobic programming.

backend_records_to_create.title: Threshold Pace Assessment
backend_records_to_create.summary: Use recent race data or a safe coach-selected threshold-style test to anchor aerobic, threshold, and triathlon swim zones.

backend_records_to_create.title: Split Consistency Assessment
backend_records_to_create.summary: Assess whether the swimmer can repeat target splits with stable stroke count and RPE before prescribing advanced pacing strategies.

backend_records_to_create.title: Race-Pace Repeatability Assessment
backend_records_to_create.summary: Check whether an advanced swimmer can hit race-pace fragments repeatedly without large speed drop or technique collapse.

backend_records_to_create.title: Dryland Event Support Rule
backend_records_to_create.summary: Dryland supports swimming through shoulder/scapular endurance, trunk control, mobility, posterior-chain strength, and power without disrupting key water sessions.

backend_records_to_create.title: Masters Swimmer Adjustment
backend_records_to_create.summary: Use more recovery, conservative volume jumps, explicit shoulder monitoring, and careful high-intensity density for adult masters swimmers.

backend_records_to_create.title: Return After Break Adjustment
backend_records_to_create.summary: Returning swimmers should restart below previous volume and intensity, re-establish feel and breathing, avoid paddles early, and progress only if symptoms stay stable.

backend_records_to_create.title: Hybrid Athlete Swim Adjustment
backend_records_to_create.summary: For athletes also lifting, running, cycling, or playing field sports, swim load must be integrated with total shoulder, trunk, and systemic fatigue.

backend_records_to_create.title: Meet Event Priority Rule
backend_records_to_create.summary: For multi-event meets, identify primary, secondary, and training events so warm-up, cool-down, pacing, and recovery match the goal.

backend_records_to_create.title: Race Warm-Up Familiarity Rule
backend_records_to_create.summary: Race warm-ups should be familiar, event-relevant, and short enough not to create fatigue. New warm-up experiments belong in training, not race day.
